summary: Details how SIP uses DNS to turn a SIP URI into the address, port and transport of the next hop, and to let a server find a backup client. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3263 explains how a SIP client uses DNS to turn a SIP address into the details needed to contact the next server. It also explains how a server can use DNS to send a response to a backup client when the original route fails.

questions: how does sip find a server

subtitle: How SIP uses DNS to find a server address, port, and transport for a request.

tldr.problem: A SIP client often has a domain name but needs to find a server's IP address, port, and transport, including alternatives when a server fails.
tldr.mechanism: NAPTR records can identify supported transports and preferences; SRV records list servers with priority and weight; A or AAAA records supply IP addresses. SIP defines how to try the resulting choices and how servers use DNS for response failover.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3263 replaces the location procedures in RFC 2543. It has been updated by RFC 7984 and RFC 8553.

today: RFC 3263 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2002 and replaces the server-location rules of RFC 2543. It has been updated by RFC 7984 and RFC 8553.

sections.title: The Server-Location Problem
sections.content:
SIP clients send requests to user agents or proxy servers. When a proxy forwards a request to another domain, it needs to identify a server there. RFC 3263 specifies DNS procedures for discovering the next hop's IP address, port, and transport protocol.

DNS also helps a server find a backup client for a response if the original client fails after sending a request. This matters because some SIP responses can take time while a person decides whether to accept a call.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP request starts with a name, but sending it requires a reachable server address and transport. DNS lookup rules help the client find that server and help a server find a response route if the first one fails.

sections.title: What DNS Must Tell the Client
sections.content:
The client needs a supported transport, an IP address, and a port. SIP can use UDP, TCP, and SCTP; TLS is defined for TCP in this RFC. DNS records can also list server priorities and weights, allowing a domain to publish several possible servers.

A client has limited time to complete call setup, so it cannot continuously test every server. It tries candidates in a defined order and may cache which server answered. The same DNS procedures support backup routing for a response when a client-side connection fails.
sections.plainLanguage: The client needs three pieces of connection information: transport, address, and port. DNS can list several servers and their order, so the client has alternatives when one does not respond.

sections.title: Selecting the Transport
sections.content:
If a SIP URI specifies a transport, the client should use it. If the target is a numeric IP address or the URI gives an explicit port without a transport, the default is UDP for SIP and TCP for SIPS, subject to SIP requirements for a particular request.

Otherwise, the client queries NAPTR records for the domain. The service values identify SIP or SIPS and a transport: D2U means UDP, D2T means TCP, and D2S means SCTP. The client keeps services it supports; a client resolving SIPS must discard services that do not specify SIPS. If no NAPTR records exist, it queries SRV records for its supported transports.
sections.plainLanguage: The URI may name the transport directly. If it does not, the client checks DNS for the transports the domain offers and selects one both sides support.

sections.title: Finding Servers and Trying Alternatives
sections.content:
Once the transport is known, the client uses a numeric address directly or looks up a hostname. With an explicit port, it queries A or AAAA records and tries the returned addresses. Without a port, it queries SRV records and follows their priority and weight rules. If no SRV records are found, it falls back to A or AAAA records and the transport's default port.

For SIP, a failed attempt includes a 503 response, a transport failure, or a transaction timeout with no response. The client should create a new request with a different Via branch identifier and try the next server. A transaction's retransmissions, non-2xx INVITE ACK, and CANCEL must continue to go to the server first contacted successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: After learning the transport, the client uses DNS to find candidate addresses and ports. If a server fails, the client can try the next candidate, while keeping follow-up messages for an active transaction on the same server.

sections.title: Response Failover and Backup URIs
sections.content:
A server normally sends a response over the connection that carried the request, or to the request's source address and Via port for an unreliable transport. If that route fails, it examines the top Via field and uses an IP address directly, looks up A or AAAA records for a hostname with a port, or queries SRV records for a hostname without a port.

For a URI that must reach a particular proxy, using a domain with SRV records can provide a preferred server and backup servers. This gives responses a route to another client when the original address is no longer available.
sections.plainLanguage: If the return route fails, the server checks the Via field and uses DNS to find another address. A domain name with backup SRV entries can also let a SIP URI reach an alternate server.

sections.title: DNS Changes and Transport Security
sections.content:
An attacker who changes NAPTR records could try to make a client select a less secure transport. A SIPS URI limits this risk because it must use TLS; removing DNS records can block communication but cannot make SIPS use an insecure transport. A client that regularly contacts a domain should remember whether its records included SIPS and may alert or reject a later unexpected change.

Proxies often perform the DNS lookup on a client's behalf, so the client depends on the proxy to follow the security rules. The RFC notes that a proxy that ignores SIPS records can still downgrade security.
sections.plainLanguage: Changed DNS information can affect which transport a client chooses. SIPS requires TLS, and remembering earlier secure DNS results can help a client notice an unexpected change.
